newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka says has option of referendum on devolution.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka says has option of referendum on devolution.

text.p: The Sri Lankan government retains the option of a national referendum on the constitution if its reform proposals aimed at ending a protracted ethnic war are not accepted by other parties, a senior minister said on Thursday.
"A non-binding referendum is an option that is available to the government," Minister for Justice and Constitutional Affairs Gamini Peiris told a news conference.
But he added that the People's Alliance government would do all it could to create a consensus among major political parties on the draft constitution before going to the people.
"If all that fails then the government will go to the people and ask them what they feel about it. It is the people who have to decide what they want," Peiris said.

The new constitution is being debated by a parliamentary select committee, but the process has slowed down due to disagreements between Tamil and Moslem parties, and between the main opposition United National Party (UNP) and the government.
The committee is negotiating key issues such as devolution of power to minorities and the demarcation of proposed new councils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
Sri Lanka is waging a 13-year-old war against Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, who demand a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of the island.

Peiris criticised some political parties for their reluctance to discuss the provisions in the draft constitution until the LTTE were involved in negotiations, and said the UNP had yet to state its position on the proposals.

The UNP has said it will comment on the draft constitution once it is complete. The mainstream Tamil United Liberation Front has said the LTTE have to be involved in negotiations if reforms are to be implemented.
Other Tamil parities, which support the government, have complained over the delay in implementation of the reforms, saying this would lead to an intensification of the ethnic war.
"Major political parties in parliament have a duty by the people of this country to state clearly what their ideas are on the resolution of the ethnic conflict," Peiris said.
"We will talk to the UNP. If they tell us what their reservations are, we will try and incorporate them. There will be no stone left unturned to get the support of the major political parties."
But he said the government wanted to talk to the LTTE only on condition that the rebels laid down their arms and agreed to a definite time frame for negotiations.
Peiris also said all political parties would first have to work out the parameters within which a solution to the ethnic problem could be negotiated with the LTTE.

President Chandrika Kumaratunga's government opened peace talks with the LTTE after winning power in the 1994 general election. But the talks broke down after the rebels sank two navy boats in the eastern Trincomalee harbour in April 1995.
"We have to reduce the military strength of LTTE, and then from that position of strength implement the devolution proposals," Peiris said.
A two-day meeting of PA legislators earlier this week backed Kumaratunga's proposal that the offensive against the LTTE should continue parallel to devolution.
Peiris said the PA would soon launch a campaign asking the people to support the government's initiative.
